_comment: pink - mid-tone magenta ink on a LIGHT worksheet. The inverse of midnight.
Every other coloured recipe here (midnight, sunset) tints for a dark
background, where a dim ink still reads. This theme's worksheet.bg is
0.832/0.5358/0.7001 - a bright pink of relative luminance 0.35 - and that
inverts the arithmetic. Measured against it:
stock white ink           2.62:1
this theme's magenta      3.02:1
so a paler set would be *less* legible than the set it replaces, and the
ink has to go the other way. The target is (150,30,95): a mid-tone magenta
at 3.02:1, better than stock and still unmistakably pink.
MECHANISM. Two ops, and both are load-bearing - the one that looks like it
does the work cannot do the job alone. `tint` normalises its target to unit
brightness (icons.py:451), so it can only ever make ink dimmer than white;
it can never produce dark ink. Tinting to (150,30,95) on its own lands
full-strength white pixels on (255,51,161), a hot pink at 1.28:1, i.e.
invisible on this background. The brightness pass is what sets the level,
which is why the general tint is written at full strength as (255,51,161)
and multiplied down to the target, and why the factor is 150/255. That is
the general ink's own value, not a taste judgement.
ON ORDERING. Recolouring ops replace and run on the ORIGINAL image, while
adjusting ops accumulate in recipe order on top (icons.py:747). So the
single global brightness listed last applies to every icon - which is
exactly what the second half of this recipe relies on.
WHY THE GENERAL TINT IS A LIST OF GLOBS AND NOT `*`. The set is not one
population, it is two, and they need opposite treatment:
* 85 glyphs with neutral ink - white, or a dim semi-transparent grey,
where value alone carries the lit/unlit distinction (ViewerOn is
(101,101,101) against ViewerOnBright's (202,202,202), NoCook sits at
(103,103,103) where Cook is black). These get the magenta. Because tint
scales with luminance, every one of those distinctions survives it
intact. `solid` would flatten all of them away.
* 11 glyphs already dark and already coloured. Measured, every one has
no opaque pixel above luma 184, and ErrorFace, ErrorNetwork and
OriginX are 100% dark with no bright detail anywhere. For those, a tint
is not a recolour at all - it is `colour x luma`, and their luma is
tiny, so ErrorFace's (102,0,0) would land on (13,2,2). Black. The hue
they exist to signal would be gone, and a black error badge is worse
than no signal at all. So they are left untinted and take only the
global brightness, which is a pure multiply: hue preserved exactly,
and on a light background darker is the legible direction, so they
*gain* contrast (ErrorFace 5.13:1 -> 8.51:1).
The excluded eleven are the error faces, the warning faces, the Origin axes
and the two ShowDock error states - the same semantic groups midnight and
sunset paint back, for the same reason: a red error badge is a warning to
the operator, and recolouring it to match the theme removes the signal
along with the hue. This recipe differs in how it protects them. Those two
recipes re-tint the group over the general tint, which works for them
because their backgrounds are dark and the result is still a legible hue.
Here it cannot work at all: a tint cannot brighten, so no re-tint of a
dark icon can undo the crush - the arithmetic caps it below 13/255. They
have to be excluded from the tint rather than corrected after it.
The Origin axes keep their stock red/green/blue, so X is still red. A pink
X axis is not a theme detail, it is a wrong label. This is the one place
this recipe departs from its siblings, both of which let the general tint
swallow the axes.
The cost of the glob list is that it is a maintenance liability, and it is
worth being blunt about. A new icon from a TouchDesigner update lands
untinted by default if its name does not match any pattern below, and an
untinted white glyph on a bright pink worksheet is close to invisible. The
alternative - `*` plus a group re-tint - is worse, because it silently
blackens every dark icon a future build might add. So a new icon wants a
pattern added here, and `tdthememaker diff pink` will show it as
pixel-identical to the baseline, which is the signal to look for.
CommentOnSmall is the one deliberate inclusion among the coloured glyphs:
its blue is not a signal the way an error badge is, and tinting it magenta
makes it consistent with the other 25 C* comment glyphs, which are all
neutral and would go magenta anyway.
The three pure-black glyphs - Cook, Grid, CommentOffSmall, with CookNone
and CookParentNone within 66/255 of them - cannot move under either op:
there is no hue in a black pixel, and brightness multiplies zero by
anything. That is the right outcome rather than a gap. On a light
background they are now the darkest ink in the set instead of the
exception, so they read better here than they do shipped.
No compensating factor for the four 256x256 overlays, which was the
obvious thing to add and turned out not to be needed. Measured, they cover
100% of their area but are a faint wash: 96% of their pixels sit at alpha
23, with the high-alpha pixels numbering in the dozens. Tinted to the
general magenta at alpha 23 they composite to (206,125,168) on this
background against (212,137,179) unthemed - a 2% shift. They were already
subtle, and a factor would only have reached the sparse detail.
The two badge overlays are the exception and do get the group hue, so an
error badge and its wash stay the same colour. `Error*Overlay` and
`Warn*Overlay` rather than `Error*` and `Warn*`: fnmatch matches the whole
stem, so the narrower patterns are what keeps them off the 100%-dark faces.
